etymology: From task, through the Old French tasche and Late Latin tasca, “an imposed piece of work,” joined to master; rendering the Hebrew sar mas, “chief of the levy,” the officer set over forced labour to exact the appointed quota.
biblical_def: Taskmasters are the officers Pharaoh set over Israel to break them by labour: “Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens” (Exo 1:11). The word carries its own purpose in it — the task is not work but affliction, labour weaponized, the quota used as a whip. Under them Israel built Pithom and Raamses, made brick and morter, and served with rigour (Exo 1:14). When Moses came with the word of the LORD, Pharaoh did not relent but tightened the screw, commanding the taskmasters to withhold the straw and hold the tale of bricks unchanged (Exo 5:6-10), so that the first fruit of the promise of deliverance was heavier bondage. This is God’s ordinary way: the yoke is felt as intolerable just before it is broken. And the whole account turns on a sentence spoken at the bush: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows” (Exo 3:7). The LORD is not a distant observer of the brickyard; He sees, He hears, He knows, and He comes down to deliver. Egypt therefore stands in Scripture as the standing type of sin’s dominion, and the taskmaster as the figure of a bondage no man breaks by his own arm — broken instead by a lamb slain, blood on the door, and a redeemed people led out by a mediator.
webster_summary: One who imposes tasks; an overseer of forced labour who exacts the appointed work, especially the Egyptian officers set over Israel.
webster_full: TASKMASTER, one who imposes a task, or burdens with labor.
An overseer set over laborers to exact from them a stated quantity of work.
From task, Late Latin tasca, a fixed portion of labor imposed; and master.
In Scripture, the officers Pharaoh appointed over the Israelites (Exo 1:11; 5:6).
Figuratively, any oppressive authority that exacts labor without mercy.
scriptures: Exo 1:11
Therefore they did set over them taskmasters to afflict them with their burdens. And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.
Exo 3:7
And the LORD said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows;
Exo 5:6
And Pharaoh commanded the same day the taskmasters of the people, and their officers, saying,
Exo 5:10
And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw.
corruption_summary: The Exodus is lifted out of its own book and used as a generic template of political liberation — a story about oppressors and the oppressed with the lamb, the blood, and the wrath of God quietly removed.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation theology, from Gutiérrez and Boff in the 1960s and 70s onward, made the taskmasters of Egypt the master-key of the whole Bible: God is read as the one who takes sides in a struggle between the powerful and the “marginalized,” and salvation is read as the overturning of unjust structures. Every congregation that has heard the Exodus preached as a template for a political programme has met the corruption, whether the preacher knew the name or not. The rebuttal is not to deny that God hates oppression — He says plainly that He heard their cry and knew their sorrows — but to insist that the text itself refuses the reduction. Israel did not walk out of Egypt because the oppressed rose up. Israel walked out because a lamb was killed in every house and its blood struck on the lintel, and the LORD said, when I see the blood, I will pass over you. The destroyer went through Egypt and through Goshen alike; the only difference was blood. An Exodus preached without Exo 12 has removed the very thing that made the night of deliverance safe for Israel, and has made God the ally of a faction rather than the judge of all men.

Recover the true magnitude of the deliverance by letting the New Testament name it. On the mount of transfiguration Moses and Elias “spake of his decease which he should accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luk 9:31) — and the word is exodus. The brickyard was a real bondage and a real cruelty; God really did break it; and it was all along the shadow of a greater going-out, accomplished not at the Red Sea but at a cross, delivering not from Pharaoh but from sin, death, and the wrath to come. That is why the taskmaster is a doctrinal figure and not merely a historical one. Every man out of Christ serves a harder master than the one at Pithom, who sets a quota no man ever fills and gives no straw; and no revolution has ever emancipated a soul. To read the Exodus rightly is to hear Exo 3:7 as the compassion of a God who saw, and Exo 12 as the price at which He acted, and to look from both to the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world.
roots_summary: Hebrew sar mas (“chief of the tribute-levy”), the officer of corvée labour; mas is the forced levy itself, and the root sense is exaction rather than employment.
roots_lines: Hebrew — sarey missim (שרי מסים), “princes of the levies,” Exo 1:11; the officers over forced labour.
Hebrew — mas (מס), a compulsory levy of workmen or tribute, distinct from hired service.
Hebrew — nogesim (נגשים), “drivers, exactors,” the word behind taskmasters in Exo 5:6; the same root describes the oppressor in Isa 9:4.
Greek (LXX) — ergodiōktēs, “work-driver,” a compound coined to render the Hebrew exactor.
English — task (Late Latin tasca, an imposed portion) + master; the Authorized Version keeps the note of exaction, not of employment.
usage: “Pharaoh’s taskmasters withheld the straw and kept the tale of bricks, and so the deliverance began with a heavier yoke.”
“Sin is the hardest taskmaster of all: it sets a quota no man fills and pays its servants in death.”
“The word at the bush answers every brickyard — I have seen, I have heard, I know their sorrows.”

etymology: From the Latin porta, “a gate,” through Old French portier; a gatekeeper or doorkeeper — not to be confounded with the other porter, a bearer of burdens, which comes from portare, “to carry.”
biblical_def: A porter in the Authorized Version is a doorkeeper: the man set at the gate to open, to shut, and to watch. In the house of the LORD it was a genuine standing office, not a menial errand. The porters are named by name — “Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman” (1Ch 9:17) — ordained in their set office by David and Samuel the seer, ranged by lot to the four quarters of the house, lodging round about it, opening it every morning and keeping the vessels and the chambers and the treasuries. Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was “porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation” (1Ch 9:21). The office is dignified because the door is; what a man is trusted to guard measures the honour of his trust. City gates had their porters too (2Ki 7:10; 2Sa 18:26), and the sheepfold its own: “To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice” (Joh 10:3). Then the Lord turns the office into a charge upon the whole church. The man taking a far journey “gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch” (Mar 13:34). Christ is gone into a far country; His house is left with work assigned and a door to keep; and the porter’s single duty until the Master returns is wakefulness.
webster_summary: A doorkeeper or gatekeeper; one who has charge of a gate or door, to open, shut, and guard it — a settled office in the house of the LORD.
webster_full: PORTER, a man who has the charge of a door or gate; a doorkeeper.
From the Latin porta, a gate, through the French portier.
Distinguished from porter, a carrier of burdens, which is from the Latin portare, to carry.
In Scripture, an appointed officer of the temple, ordained by David and Samuel (1Ch 9:17-27).
Figuratively, one charged to watch at the door until the master returns (Mar 13:34).
scriptures: And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;
And Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was porter of the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.
For the Son of man is as a man taking a far journey, who left his house, and gave authority to his servants, and to every man his work, and commanded the porter to watch.
Joh 10:3
To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.
corruption_summary: The ordinary offices of Christ’s house are despised from two sides at once — swallowed up by a clerical caste that makes the pastor a priest, or dissolved altogether by a churchmanship that will own no office and no door.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome answered the question of office by inventing a priesthood: a mediating order with sacrificing power, a hierarchy rising to a single head, and beneath it a laity that receives rather than serves. The Reformation called the church back from that corruption to the New Testament pattern — two offices, elder and deacon, exercised in a local congregation, with a plurality of elders and no order of men standing between the believer and his Lord. But the opposite error is now the livelier one. A great deal of modern churchmanship treats every office as a relic of institutionalism: no ordination, no roll, no discipline, no doorkeeper, on the theory that structure quenches the Spirit. Scripture knows nothing of it. The porters of 1Ch 9 were named, numbered, genealogically reckoned, lodged by lot at the four quarters, and answerable for the vessels by tale. A house of God without offices is not more spiritual than one with them; it is only one with no one accountable when the door stands open.

Recover the porter as the plain picture of ordinary faithfulness. His work is unglamorous: he opens in the morning, he keeps the keys, he watches. He does not preach, he does not sing, he is not named in the psalms he guards the door for. Yet the Lord Himself chose that office to describe the posture of the whole church between the ascension and the coming: authority given, work assigned to every man, and the porter commanded to watch (Mar 13:34). The charge is not to speculate about the hour but to be awake at the post when the door is knocked upon. Let elders keep doctrine, deacons keep mercy, and every member keep his own assigned work, and the house will be found in order at whatever watch the Master comes — at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew sho'er, gatekeeper, from sha'ar, a gate; Greek thurōros, door-watcher, from thura, a door — in both tongues the man is named from the thing he keeps.
roots_lines: Hebrew — sho'er (שוער), gatekeeper, from sha'ar (שער), a gate; the temple porters of 1Ch 9 and 26.
Greek — thurōros (θυρωρóς), doorkeeper, from thura, a door, and ouros, a watcher (Joh 10:3).
Latin — portarius, from porta, a gate; the source of the English word by way of Old French portier.
Homonym — the burden-bearing porter is from Latin portare, to carry, and is a wholly separate word.
Sense — the office joins two duties that always go together in Scripture: to open to the sheep, and to shut against the thief.
usage: “The porters were ordained in their set office, and every gate had its man by name.”
“He commanded the porter to watch — which is to say, He left His church awake at the door.”
“To the true Shepherd the porter openeth; the thief must climb up some other way.”

etymology: From the Latin praesidens, present participle of praesidere, “to sit before, to preside over” (prae, before + sedere, to sit); the Authorized Version’s rendering of the Aramaic sarekin, the three chief officers over Darius’s hundred and twenty princes.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version the word belongs to one chapter. Darius set a hundred and twenty princes over his kingdom, “and over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first” (Dan 6:2), that the princes might give accounts to them and the king have no damage. The office is civil, administrative, and pagan — an audit against corruption in a heathen empire — and a believing Jew held the first place in it. That is the first lesson: Daniel served Babylon and then Persia with such diligence that his enemies could find no occasion against him “concerning the kingdom” (Dan 6:4). His faithfulness to God made him the better servant of the state, not the worse. The second lesson follows immediately. Unable to fault his administration, the presidents and princes contrived a law that made prayer to God a capital crime and carried it to the king by flattery (Dan 6:7). Daniel did not organize resistance, did not revile the king, did not flee; he went into his house, opened his windows toward Jerusalem, and prayed as he did aforetime. He then bore the sentence. Here is the whole Christian doctrine of the magistrate in one man: honour the powers that be as ordained of God, obey them in everything lawful, and when they command what God forbids, disobey openly and suffer quietly, for we ought to obey God rather than men.
webster_summary: Officers who preside; in Scripture, the three chief ministers over Darius’s princes, of whom Daniel was first.
webster_full: PRESIDENT, one who is elected or appointed to preside over a body of men, and to direct their proceedings.
From the Latin praesidens, sitting before or over; prae, before, and sedere, to sit.
An officer set over others to receive their accounts and to guard the interest of the sovereign.
In Scripture, the three set over the hundred and twenty princes of the Persian realm (Dan 6:2).
Also, in later use, the chief magistrate of a republic or the head of a corporation.
scriptures: Dan 6:2
And over these three presidents; of whom Daniel was first: that the princes might give accounts unto them, and the king should have no damage.
Dan 6:3
Then this Daniel was preferred above the presidents and princes, because an excellent spirit was in him; and the king thought to set him over the whole realm.
Dan 6:4

Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.
Dan 6:7

All the presidents of the kingdom, the governors, and the princes, the counsellors, and the captains, have consulted together to establish a royal statute, and to make a firm decree, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any God or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.
corruption_summary: Romans 13 is distorted in two directions at once — a contempt for lawful authority that makes every ordinance of man optional, and a statolatry that hands the magistrate the conscience which belongs to Christ alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The first distortion treats civil authority as a nuisance to be evaded wherever it can be evaded, and reads every inconvenient law as tyranny. Scripture does not permit it. The powers that be are ordained of God; the magistrate is His minister, a terror not to good works but to the evil; and the Christian is to be subject not only for wrath but for conscience sake, paying tribute, custom, fear, and honour where each is due. Daniel gave Darius an administration so clean that a hostile audit found nothing. The second distortion is graver because it wears the language of obedience: it takes Rom 13 to mean that whatever the magistrate commands, the Christian must do, and so grants to the state a jurisdiction over the conscience that God has reserved to Himself. The 1689 Confession is exact here — God alone is Lord of the conscience, and to obey men against His word is to betray liberty of conscience and right reason. The decree of Dan 6 was perfectly lawful by Persian process, sealed by the king, unalterable by the law of the Medes and Persians, and utterly void before God the moment it forbade prayer.

Recover the limit and the manner together, for men usually lose one in seizing the other. The limit is Act 5:29 — “We ought to obey God rather than men” — and it is not a general licence to disobey what we dislike but a narrow and absolute refusal at the point where obedience to man requires sin against God. The manner is Daniel’s: no conspiracy, no contempt, no lie, no attempt to escape the penalty. He opened his windows and prayed where he could be seen, and then went down into the den without railing at the king who sent him there. That is Christian civil courage — open in the duty, submissive under the punishment, and content to leave the vindication with God, who shut the lions’ mouths and made a pagan emperor publish His name throughout all the earth.
roots_summary: Aramaic sarekin, chief officers, likely from an Old Persian root for “head”; Latin praesidere, to sit before — the presiding officer who receives account from those beneath him.
roots_lines: Aramaic — sarekin (סרכין), chief ministers, Dan 6:2; a Persian loanword in the Aramaic of Daniel.
Persian — the underlying sense is one set at the head, an overseer of satraps in the imperial administration.
Latin — praesidere, to sit before or preside; whence praesidens and the English president.
Related — princes in Dan 6 renders achashdarpenayya, the satraps, the hundred and twenty under the three.
Sense — the office is one of audit and account, which is why an incorruptible man was hated in it.
usage: “Daniel was first of the three presidents, and his enemies could find no fault in the accounts.”
“The decree was lawful by Persian process and void before God the moment it forbade prayer.”
“Open in the duty, submissive under the penalty — that is the Daniel pattern for a Christian under an unjust statute.”

etymology: From the Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum, “a fortified place or camp,” through Anglo-Saxon castel; in the Authorized Version it renders several words — a stronghold, a fortified tower, an encampment of tents, and the Roman barracks at Jerusalem.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses castle for any fortified holding, and the sense shifts with the setting. Among the sons of Ishmael it means fortified encampments — “by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations” (Gen 25:16). Of Jerusalem it means the Jebusite citadel that David took: “Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David” (1Ch 11:5) — the stronghold that had been counted impregnable, seized and made the seat of the LORD’s anointed. In the Acts it is the Antonia, the Roman barracks overlooking the temple court, into which Paul was carried when the multitude would have torn him in pieces (Act 21:34; Act 23:10). There the apostle stood on the stairs and preached to the mob that had just tried to kill him, and there the Lord stood by him in the night and said, Be of good cheer. The military sense of the word underlies its great spiritual use. Israel knew what walls were for, and knew that walls fail: horses and chariots and high towers are a vain thing for safety. So Solomon sets the true fortress over against every stone one: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). The believer’s castle is not a place but a Person, and the gate is never shut against him.
webster_summary: A fortified building or stronghold; also a fortified encampment, and in the Acts the Roman barracks at Jerusalem into which Paul was taken.
webster_full: CASTLE, a house fortified for defense against an enemy; a fortress.
From the Latin castellum, a diminutive of castrum, a fortified camp.
In Scripture, sometimes a walled encampment of a nomadic people (Gen 25:16).
The stronghold of Zion, taken by David from the Jebusites (1Ch 11:5).
In the Acts, the fortress adjoining the temple where the Roman garrison lay (Act 21:34).
scriptures: These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names, by their towns, and by their castles; twelve princes according to their nations.
And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, Thou shalt not come hither. Nevertheless David took the castle of Zion, which is the city of David.
And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle.

And when there arose a great dissension, the chief captain, fearing lest Paul should have been pulled in pieces of them, commanded the soldiers to go down, and to take him by force from among them, and to bring him into the castle.
corruption_summary: No postmodern redefinition attaches to the word; the live danger is the old one of trusting the wall instead of the LORD, and of mistaking a place of safety for the source of it.
corruption_paragraphs: The abiding temptation the word exposes is trust misplaced in defences. Judah looked to the armour of the house of the forest, to the waters of the lower pool, to the strength of walls, and did not look unto the maker thereof. Every age builds its castle and calls it security — a fortified savings, a fortified reputation, a fortified household, a fortified nation — and every castle in Scripture eventually falls to someone. Even the castle of Zion, taken by David and made the city of the great King, was afterwards broken down and burned when the people within it forsook the covenant. The wall is not wicked; the trust is. Nehemiah built walls and prayed; David took the stronghold and sang that the LORD was his rock and his fortress. The sin is not fortification but the quiet transfer of confidence from the LORD of hosts to the works of our hands.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the only impregnable stronghold in Scripture is a name. “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10) — and notice the two things required, that the man be righteous and that he run. The tower does not shelter those who admire it from a distance; it shelters those who flee into it, which is exactly what faith does with Christ. Notice also that Paul’s safest night in Jerusalem was spent as a prisoner inside a pagan garrison, because the Lord who stood by him was his real defence and used a Roman fortress as an instrument. God can make a castle of anything, or of nothing. The saints have been safest in dens and caves and have perished in citadels; the difference has never been the masonry.
roots_summary: Latin castellum from castrum, a fortified camp; behind the English lie Hebrew tirah (an encircled encampment), metsudah (a stronghold), and Greek parembolē (the barracks or camp).
roots_lines: Hebrew — tirah (טירה), an encampment ringed with stone or tents, rendered castles in Gen 25:16.
Hebrew — metsudah (מצודה), a stronghold or fastness; the castle of Zion in 1Ch 11:5, and the psalmist’s word for God Himself.
Hebrew — birah (בירה), a palace-fortress, used of the temple citadel in 1Ch 29:1 and of Shushan the palace.
Greek — parembolē (παρεμβολή), a camp or barracks; the Antonia fortress in Act 21–23.
Latin — castellum, diminutive of castrum; the same root gives English chester in place-names.
usage: “David took the castle of Zion, and the place men called impregnable became the city of the king.”
“Paul preached from the stairs of the castle to the very mob that had dragged him out of the temple.”
“A man may lose every wall he has built and still be safe, if he has run into the name of the LORD.”

etymology: From the Old French parleur, “a room for speaking,” from parler, to speak (Late Latin parabolare, from parabola, a discourse); the Authorized Version’s word for a private inner chamber where a man received guests or withdrew alone.
biblical_def: A parlour in the Authorized Version is an inner room set apart — a chamber for private speech, a place of retirement from the public rooms of a house. Eglon king of Moab sat in a summer parlour which he had for himself alone, and there Ehud came to him with the words, I have a message from God unto thee; and when the deed was done Ehud “went forth through the porch, and shut the doors of the parlour upon him, and locked them” (Jdg 3:23), so that the servants waited outside till they were ashamed, and opened at last upon their lord fallen down dead (Jdg 3:25). The private chamber, chosen for safety, became the place of judgment. Elsewhere the word is honourable. Samuel took Saul and his servant “and brought them into the parlour, and made them sit in the chiefest place among them that were bidden” (1Sa 9:22) — the inner chamber of the high place, where the man God had chosen was seated before he knew what he was chosen for. And when David gave Solomon the pattern of the house, the inner parlours were part of it (1Ch 28:11), which is the weightiest use of all: the pattern was not Solomon’s invention but delivered, room by room, by the Spirit, so that even the private chambers of the LORD’s house were built by revelation and not by taste.
webster_summary: An inner or private room for speech and retirement; in Scripture a withdrawing chamber, and among the chambers of the temple pattern given to Solomon.
webster_full: PARLOR, primarily, a room in monasteries where the religious met for conversation.
In modern usage, the room in a house appropriated to the entertainment of company.
From the French parler, to speak; Late Latin parabolare, to discourse.
In Scripture, an inner chamber of retirement, as Eglon’s summer parlour (Jdg 3:20-25).
Also the inner chambers of the temple, in the pattern David delivered to Solomon (1Ch 28:11).
scriptures: Jdg 3:23
Then Ehud went forth through the porch, and shut the doors of the parlour upon him, and locked them.
Jdg 3:25
And they tarried till they were ashamed: and, behold, he opened not the doors of the parlour; therefore they took a key, and opened them: and, behold, their lord was fallen down dead on the earth.
And Samuel took Saul and his servant, and brought them into the parlour, and made them sit in the chiefest place among them that were bidden, which were about thirty persons.

Then David gave to Solomon his son the pattern of the porch, and of the houses thereof, and of the treasuries thereof, and of the upper chambers thereof, and of the inner parlours thereof, and of the place of the mercy seat,
corruption_summary: No modern redefinition has fallen on the word; what needs recovering is the doctrine the inner chambers carry — that God’s house is built by His pattern, and that no private room hides a man from Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is not lexical but practical: the assumption that a private room is a place where a man is unobserved and unaccountable. Eglon had a summer parlour which he had for himself alone, locked, comfortable, and guarded — and it proved the one place in Moab where the judgment of God found him with no servant at hand. The believer’s closet is the counterpart. Christ commands the shut door for prayer, and He grounds it on the same fact from the other side: thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly. The same walls that make a chamber private to men make it a place where God alone is witness, and that cuts both ways. Whatever a man does in his inner room, whether he prays there or sins there, he does before the face of God, and the door he locks shuts out only creatures.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pattern. When David handed Solomon the plan of the porch, the treasuries, the upper chambers and the inner parlours, he added that the LORD made him understand in writing by His hand upon him, all the works of this pattern. Not one chamber of the house of God was left to human preference. That principle governs worship still: what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted in the worship of His house. Men who would never think of adding a room to Solomon’s temple add whole wings to the worship of the New Testament church without a syllable of warrant, and call it liberty. The parlour of 1Ch 28:11 is a quiet witness against them — even the private rooms were given by revelation.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'aliyyah, a roof-chamber or upper room, and lishkah, a hall or chamber of the sanctuary; the English comes by way of French parler, a room appointed for speech.
roots_lines: Hebrew — 'aliyyah (עלייה), an upper chamber on the roof, cool in summer; Eglon’s summer parlour (Jdg 3:20).
Hebrew — lishkah (לשכה), a chamber or hall attached to a sanctuary; the parlour of 1Sa 9:22.
Hebrew — chadar (חדר), an inner room; the word behind the inner parlours of the temple pattern.
French — parleur, from parler, to speak; originally the room in a religious house where speech was allowed.
Latin — parabolare, to discourse, from parabola, a comparison or speech; the same root gives parable and palaver.
usage: “Eglon sat in his summer parlour alone, and heard the last message he would ever hear.”
“Samuel set Saul in the chiefest place of the parlour before the young man knew he was a king.”
“Even the inner parlours of the house were in the pattern — God left no room of His worship to our invention.”

etymology: From the Anglo-Saxon galga, a cross or gibbet; in Esther it renders the Hebrew 'ets, “tree” or “timber,” the Persian stake of fifty cubits on which Haman purposed to hang Mordecai and on which he was himself hanged.
biblical_def: The gallows of Scripture belongs to the book of Esther, and it is the hinge on which the whole providence of that book turns. Haman, full of wrath because one Jew would not bow, was counselled by his wife and friends: “Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon” (Est 5:14). The thing pleased him, and he built it — seventy-five feet of deliberate spite, raised in his own courtyard so that the whole city might see his enemy die. That same night the king could not sleep, and the book of the records was read, and Haman was made to lead through the street the man he had come to destroy. Then Harbonah, who had noticed the timber standing in Haman’s house, named it before the king (Est 7:9), and the sentence came in five words: Hang him thereon. “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Est 7:10). Afterward his ten sons were hanged upon it also (Est 9:25). The name of God is never spoken in Esther, and He is never absent from a line of it. The gallows is the standing monument of Psa 7:15 — “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” — and of the law that the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands.
webster_summary: An instrument of execution consisting of an upright timber, or two with a cross-beam, on which criminals are hanged; in Esther, Haman’s stake of fifty cubits.
webster_full: GALLOWS, an instrument of punishment, on which criminals are put to death by hanging.
It consists usually of two posts and a cross-beam on the top.
From the Saxon galga, a cross or gibbet; the same root appears in the Gothic galga.
In Scripture, the Hebrew is 'ets, a tree or timber, hence a stake set upright (Est 5:14).
Proverbially, the fate a man prepares for another and himself receives.
scriptures: Est 5:14

Then said Zeresh his wife and all his friends unto him, Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high, and to morrow speak thou unto the king that Mordecai may be hanged thereon: then go thou in merrily with the king unto the banquet. And the thing pleased Haman; and he caused the gallows to be made.
Est 7:9

And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon.
Est 7:10
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king’s wrath pacified.
Est 9:25

But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows.
corruption_summary: The reversal is flattened into “karma,” “poetic justice,” or mere irony — an impersonal cosmic balance replacing the God who governs sleepless nights, court records, and the tongue of a chamberlain.
corruption_paragraphs: Haman’s end is one of the best-known reversals in literature, and it is almost always told as irony: the schemer hoist with his own petard, the universe evening the score. That reading is a theft of agency. Karma is an impersonal law working through fate; providence is a Person working through second causes. Esther names none of the causes as miracles — a king’s insomnia, a reader picking one page of the chronicles, a queen’s invitation to a second banquet, a chamberlain who happened to have seen a timber in a courtyard — and every one of them lands exactly where it must for a nation to be spared and one man to be hanged. The book withholds the name of God precisely so that the reader will learn to see His hand where His name is not written, which is the ordinary condition of every day we live. To call it irony is to admire the pattern while denying the weaver.

Recover both halves of the doctrine. First, the moral government of God is real and inescapable: “He made a pit, and digged it, and is fallen into the ditch which he made” (Psa 7:15); the mischief returns upon a man’s own head and his violent dealing comes down upon his own pate. Vengeance is the LORD’s, and He does not need our help to execute it — Mordecai never lifted a hand against Haman, and neither should the Christian who is being schemed against. Second, and greater, there is one gallows in Scripture on which the innocent hung in the guilty’s room. Haman got what he deserved on his own timber; Christ took what we deserved on His, made a curse for us, as it is written, cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. Every deserved execution in Scripture points by contrast to the one undeserved death that saves, and there the wrath of the King was pacified for ever.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ets, “tree, timber,” the upright stake of Persian execution; the English word is Saxon galga, a gibbet or cross, and the Greek renders the Hebrew with the ordinary word for wood.
roots_lines: Hebrew — 'ets (עץ), tree, wood, timber; in Esther an upright stake for impaling or hanging.
Hebrew — talah (תלה), to hang up, the verb used of Haman and of the bodies exposed under Deu 21:22-23.
Greek — xulon (ξύλον), wood or tree, the New Testament word for the cross in Act 5:30 and Gal 3:13.
Saxon — galga, a gibbet or cross; the English gallows is a plural form long used as a singular.
Measure — fifty cubits is roughly seventy-five feet; the height was pride, not necessity.
usage: “He built the gallows in his own courtyard, and it was the last thing he ever built.”
“The book never names God, and there is not a page of it He is absent from.”
“Haman hung on the timber he deserved; Christ hung on one He did not.”

etymology: From the Old French obeissance, “obedience, submission,” from obeir, to obey (Latin obedire); in the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew shachah, to bow down or prostrate oneself — the bodily act by which honour is rendered.
biblical_def: Obeisance is the bow: the bodily gesture by which a man acknowledges another’s dignity or place. Scripture treats it as an ordinary and proper thing between men. Moses met his father in law and “did obeisance, and kissed him” (Exo 18:7). The princes of Judah made obeisance to the king (2Ch 24:17). It is the word of Joseph’s dreams, and there it becomes prophecy: “your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf” (Gen 37:7), and again the sun and the moon and the eleven stars (Gen 37:9) — dreams his brethren hated him for, and which God fulfilled through the very selling that was meant to prevent them. Years later, in a room in Egypt, “they bowed down their heads, and made obeisance” (Gen 43:28) to a governor they did not know was their brother. The same Hebrew word is used of worship rendered to God, and there lies the whole distinction the Bible presses. Bowing to a father, a magistrate, a master, or a king is honour and is commanded under the fifth commandment; bowing to God is worship, and He will not divide it with any creature. Mordecai would not bow to Haman, and Daniel’s friends would not bow to an image, precisely because the gesture had been claimed for what belongs to God alone.
webster_summary: A bow or act of reverence; the bodily gesture of honour rendered to a superior, and, toward God alone, of worship.
webster_full: OBEISANCE, a bow or courtesy; an act of reverence made by an inclination of the body.
From the French obeissance, obedience, from obeir, Latin obedire, to obey.
It expresses submission, respect, or civility toward a superior.
In Scripture, the Hebrew shachah, to bow down, used both of honour to men and of worship to God.
Joseph’s brethren made obeisance to him in Egypt, fulfilling his dreams (Gen 43:28).
scriptures: Gen 37:7
For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.
Gen 37:9
And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me.
And they answered, Thy servant our father is in good health, he is yet alive. And they bowed down their heads, and made obeisance.
Exo 18:7
And Moses went out to meet his father in law, and did obeisance, and kissed him; and they asked each other of their welfare; and they came into the tent.
corruption_summary: Deference itself is now treated as degrading — every bow read as servility — while the reverence withdrawn from fathers, masters and magistrates is spent lavishly on celebrities, experts, and the state.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is that no one should have to bow to anyone; that honour rendered to a superior is a relic of a servile age; that respect must be earned afresh by every officeholder or it is owed to none. Scripture will not have it. The fifth commandment attaches honour to a relation, not to a performance: honour thy father and thy mother, and by the same rule masters, elders, magistrates, and the aged. Moses bowed to Jethro; the princes bowed to the king; Joseph’s brethren bowed to a governor. None of it made them less men. And the deference that is refused where God commands it does not evaporate — it goes somewhere. A generation that will not rise up before the hoary head will queue for hours to see an entertainer, and a people that despises the ordinary authority of fathers will accept extraordinary authority from the state. Contempt of lawful honour is not the abolition of bowing but the misdirection of it.

Recover the line the Bible draws, which is not between bowing and not bowing but between honour and worship. The same word covers both, and the same body performs both, so the difference must be held by conscience and by revelation. Give honour to whom honour is due, freely, gladly, and without the sourness that measures whether a man deserves his office. But when the bow is demanded as worship — to an image, to a man in the place of God, to any creature claiming what belongs to the Creator — then it is Mordecai’s refusal, and the three in Dura’s, and the cost is to be counted and paid. Joseph’s dreams are the pattern of how God secures true honour: not seized by the man who wants it, but given by God through years of pit, prison, and forgetting, until the brethren bow at last and hear the words, I am Joseph your brother.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachah, to bow oneself down, prostrate; Greek proskuneō, to do reverence; the English comes from French obeissance, the obedience of the body made visible.
roots_lines: Hebrew — shachah (שחה), to bow down, prostrate oneself; used of honour to men and of worship to God alike.
Hebrew — qadad (קדד), to bow the head; frequently paired with shachah, as in Gen 43:28.
Greek — proskuneō (προσκυνέω), to do obeisance or worship; refused by Peter in Act 10:26 and by the angel in Rev 22:9.
French — obeissance, obedience or submission, from obeir, to obey; the outward act of an inward yielding.
Distinction — the language does not divide honour from worship; Scripture and conscience must, for God gives His glory to no other.
usage: “They bowed down their heads, and made obeisance — and the dream of the sheaves stood fulfilled.”
“Moses did obeisance to his father in law, and lost nothing of his office by it.”
“Honour to whom honour is due; but the bow that is demanded as worship must be refused whatever it costs.”

etymology: From the Old French brique, a fragment or lump, related to break; rendering the Hebrew lebenah, from laban, “to be white,” the pale mud block moulded and dried — man’s manufactured substitute for stone.
biblical_def: Brick is the first building material named in Scripture, and it is named at Babel. The men of Shinar said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly — and the narrative adds the telling clause, they had brick for stone, and slime for morter. Brick is not what God gives; it is what man makes. Stone is quarried out of creation; brick is compounded of dust and fire in a kiln, uniform, mass-produced, fit for raising a tower whose top may reach unto heaven and for making a name. Set beside it the LORD’s own instruction for His altar: if thou wilt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stone, for if thou lift up thy tool upon it, thou hast polluted it (Exo 20:25). Unhewn stone for God’s altar; burnt brick for man’s tower. Then brick becomes the very substance of bondage: Israel’s lives were made bitter with hard bondage “in morter, and in brick” (Exo 1:14), and when Pharaoh withheld the straw the officers were beaten and cried, “There is no straw given unto thy servants, and they say to us, Make brick” (Exo 5:16). And at the end the same defiance returns: “The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones” (Isa 9:10) — a people under judgment answering God with a construction plan.
webster_summary: A mass of clay moulded and hardened by fire or sun for building; in Scripture the material of Babel’s tower and of Israel’s bondage in Egypt.
webster_full: BRICK, a mass of clay tempered with water, formed into a long square, and baked or burnt in a kiln.
From the French brique, a fragment or piece; allied to break.
Bricks are used for walls and buildings where stone is scarce or costly.
In Scripture, the material of the tower of Babel, brick being used for stone (Gen 11:3).
The forced labor of the Israelites in Egypt consisted in making brick (Exo 1:14; 5:16).
scriptures: Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
Exo 5:16
There is no straw given unto thy servants, and they say to us, Make brick: and, behold, thy servants are beaten; but the fault is in thine own people.
Isa 9:10
The bricks are fallen down, but we will build with hewn stones: the sycomores are cut down, but we will change them into cedars.
Isa 65:3
A people that provoketh me to anger continually to my face; that sacrificeth in gardens, and burneth incense upon altars of brick;
corruption_summary: Babel is retold as a fable about diversity or as a myth explaining languages, and its actual sin — a manufactured ascent to heaven undertaken to make man a name — is exactly the project the modern West is still running.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misreadings compete. The first treats Gen 11 as legendary material, an etiological tale invented to explain why men speak different tongues; the second, common in pulpits, reduces it to a lesson about pride in general with no reference to the specific thing the builders wanted. Both miss the text. The builders state their own aim twice: let us build us a city and a tower whose top may reach unto heaven, and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered. It is a religious project and a political one at once — a way up to God of human manufacture, and a unity of mankind secured by concentration rather than by covenant. The brick is not incidental to it. Brick is the technology that made the tower possible: standardized, kiln-hardened, requiring no quarry, no mountain, no gift of God, only clay and fire and organized labour. Man’s religion has always preferred brick, because brick can be made to specification and stone must be received.

Recover the contrast God Himself draws, for it runs from Genesis to the cross. At Babel man builds upward with burnt brick to reach heaven and make a name; at Sinai God forbids a tool to be lifted on the stone of His altar, lest the worshipper contribute anything to the place where blood is shed for him. Every altar of brick is a work of man’s hands, which is why Isaiah lists them among the provocations of an apostate people (Isa 65:3). The gospel is the end of brickmaking. There is a stone the builders rejected which is become the head of the corner; believers are lively stones built up a spiritual house, not bricks pressed from one mould; and the name man could not make for himself at Shinar God gives freely in Christ, a new name written, to them that overcome. And the bondage of Exo 1:14 tells us where the brickyard ends: the man who insists on building his own way to heaven finishes as a slave in the morter, beaten for a quota he can never fill.
roots_summary: Hebrew lebenah, from laban, to be white — the pale sun-dried or kiln-burnt block; contrasted throughout Scripture with 'eben, stone, which is found rather than made.
roots_lines: Hebrew — lebenah (לבנה), a brick, from laban (לבן), to be white; the pale clay block of Mesopotamia and Egypt.
Hebrew — 'eben (אבן), stone, quarried and given; the material God requires for His altar, unhewn (Exo 20:25).
Hebrew — chemar (חמר), bitumen or slime, the mortar of Babel, distinguished from lime morter.
Greek (LXX) — plinthos (πλίνθος), a brick or tile; whence the English plinth.
Sense — the whole theology of the word lies in one clause of Gen 11:3: they had brick for stone.
usage: “They had brick for stone — and that clause is the history of every man-made religion since.”
“Unhewn stone for God’s altar, burnt brick for man’s tower; the two builders are never confused in Scripture.”
“Israel’s lives were made bitter in morter and in brick, and the quota never once came down.”

etymology: From the Anglo-Saxon streaw, that which is strewn; rendering the Hebrew teben, the chopped stalks of grain left after threshing — used as fodder for cattle and as the binding temper mixed into mud brick.
biblical_def: Straw is the chopped stalk left when the grain is threshed out: worthless as food for men, indispensable as fodder for beasts and as the binder that holds a mud brick together. Its great appearance in Scripture is in Pharaoh’s answer to the word of the LORD. When Moses said, Let my people go, Pharaoh charged the taskmasters, “Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw” (Exo 5:10), and the quota stood unaltered: “Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks” (Exo 5:18). So Israel “was scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw” (Exo 5:12) — the labour doubled, the standard unchanged, the officers beaten for the shortfall. It is one of the plainest pictures of tyranny in Scripture, and also one of the plainest of the law under a fallen man’s hand: a demand held at full height while the means of meeting it are taken away. Against that stands the picture at the other end of the Bible, where straw appears in the peace of the restored creation: “the lion shall eat straw like the ox” (Isa 11:7). The same humble fodder that measured Egypt’s cruelty measures the kingdom’s gentleness, when nothing in all God’s holy mountain shall hurt nor destroy.
webster_summary: The stalk of grain left after threshing, used for fodder and as the binding temper in mud brick; withheld by Pharaoh while the quota of bricks stood unchanged.
webster_full: STRAW, the stalk or stem of certain species of grain, pulse and grasses, particularly of wheat, rye, oats, barley and buckwheat.
From the Saxon streaw; that which is strewed or scattered.
It is used chiefly as fodder and litter for cattle, and formerly as a temper in unburnt brick.
In Scripture, Pharaoh withheld straw from the Israelites while requiring the same tale of bricks (Exo 5:7-18).
Proverbially, a thing of small value; but in Isaiah, the food of the lion in the peaceable kingdom (Isa 11:7).
scriptures: Exo 5:10
And the taskmasters of the people went out, and their officers, and they spake to the people, saying, Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw.
Exo 5:12
So the people were scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw.
Exo 5:18
Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks.
Isa 11:7
And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.
corruption_summary: “Bricks without straw” has been worn down into a workplace cliché for being under-resourced, emptied of the cruelty it named and of the deliverance that answered it.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase survives in ordinary speech long after its meaning has been rubbed off. Men say they are being asked to make bricks without straw when a budget is cut or a deadline is short, and the comparison is not simply false — the pattern really is the same, a demand held at full height while the means are withdrawn — but it has been made trivial. In Exodus the officers of the children of Israel were beaten daily for the shortfall; the scattering over all the land to gather stubble was added to a day’s work already brutal; and the whole device was the deliberate retaliation of a king against the word of God. It was calculated cruelty with a theological aim: Pharaoh said, Ye are idle, ye are idle, therefore ye say, Let us go and do sacrifice to the LORD — treating the desire to worship as the sloth that justified the crackdown. That is how the world has always answered a people asking leave to serve God, and it deserves a stronger word than inconvenience.

Recover what the straw teaches about law and grace. Pharaoh is the picture of a taskmaster who raises the standard and withdraws the help, and it is precisely how sin and a guilty conscience deal with a man: the demand of righteousness stands at full height, and the sinner has no means whatever of meeting it. The law given by Moses does not lower the tale of bricks by one. But God does what Pharaoh never would — He supplies in His Son everything His own law requires, so that the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit. Note also how the episode ends. The people, made worse off by the promise of deliverance, turned on Moses; Moses turned to the LORD and said, why is it that thou hast sent me? And the answer was not an explanation but a covenant name: I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians. Deliverance was never in doubt; only the timing was hidden.
roots_summary: Hebrew teben, chopped threshed stalk used for fodder and brick-temper, distinguished from qash, the stubble left standing in the field which Israel was driven to gather in its place.
roots_lines: Hebrew — teben (תבן), straw or chaff-stalk, chopped for cattle fodder and mixed as temper into mud brick.
Hebrew — qash (קש), stubble, the field-remnant Israel gathered when the straw was withheld (Exo 5:12); elsewhere a figure of what the fire consumes.
Hebrew — matkoneth (מתכנת), the measure or tale of bricks, the fixed quota held unchanged in Exo 5:8.
Saxon — streaw, that which is strewn or scattered; the same root gives English strew.
Use — without the binding straw a sun-dried brick crumbles; the withholding was a technical impossibility, not merely a hardship.
usage: “Thus saith Pharaoh, I will not give you straw — and yet ye shall deliver the tale of bricks.”
“They gathered stubble instead of straw, and were beaten for the difference.”
“The law never lowers the quota; grace supplies in Christ what the law demands.”

etymology: From the Latin pavimentum, a beaten or rammed floor, from pavire, “to beat down, to ram”; a floor of stone or tile laid over the ground — in Scripture the paved court where Israel worshipped and where Christ was judged.
biblical_def: A pavement is a laid floor of stone: the surface men stand on, kneel on, and are tried on. In the house of the LORD it is the place of prostrate worship. When the fire came down and the glory filled the house at Solomon’s dedication, all the children of Israel “bowed themselves with their faces to the ground upon the pavement, and worshipped, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever” (2Ch 7:3). Ezekiel’s visionary temple has its pavement running round the outward court with thirty chambers upon it (Eze 40:17). Ahaz, turning the temple furniture to his own purposes, took down the sea from off the brasen oxen “and put it upon a pavement of stones” (2Ki 16:17) — a small alteration that was a large apostasy, the pattern given by God quietly amended to suit a king. And then the word appears once more, in the fourth Gospel, at the hour toward which the whole temple pointed: “Pilate therefore... brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha” (Joh 19:13). On one pavement Israel fell down before the glory of God; on another the Lord of glory stood, silent, while a Roman governor took his seat to condemn Him. The same stone that receives the worshipper receives the Judge of all the earth as a prisoner.
webster_summary: A floor of stone, brick, or tile laid on the ground; in Scripture the paved court of the temple, and Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in judgment on Christ.
webster_full: PAVEMENT, a floor or covering of solid work, intended for a firm and convenient surface.
From the Latin pavimentum, from pavire, to beat or ram down.
Pavements are formed of stones, bricks, tiles, or of mosaic work.
In Scripture, the paved court of the temple where the people worshipped (2Ch 7:3).
Also the place called Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in the judgment seat (Joh 19:13).
scriptures: And when all the children of Israel saw how the fire came down, and the glory of the LORD upon the house, they bowed themselves with their faces to the ground upon the pavement, and worshipped, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever.
When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha.
And king Ahaz cut off the borders of the bases, and removed the laver from off them; and took down the sea from off the brasen oxen that were under it, and put it upon a pavement of stones.
Then brought he me into the outward court, and, lo, there were chambers, and a pavement made for the court round about: thirty chambers were upon the pavement.
corruption_summary: No modern redefinition attaches to the word; what is lost is the weight of the two pavements — the floor of adoring worship and the floor of the world’s judgment seat, and what it cost to join them.
corruption_paragraphs: The nearest thing to a live corruption here is the tendency to treat the trial before Pilate as a miscarriage of justice and nothing more — a good man destroyed by cowardly politics, which is true as far as it goes and stops well short of the gospel. Pilate’s pavement was not merely a courtroom where an innocent man was failed. It was the appointed place where the Son of God, having power to summon twelve legions, held His peace and let the sentence fall, because the sentence was the reason He came. Peter preached both truths in one breath at Pentecost: delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain. Neither cancels the other. Pilate is guilty, the rulers are guilty, and yet not one nail was driven that God had not ordained for the salvation of His people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the connection between the two floors. At the dedication the fire fell, the glory filled the house, and a whole nation went down on its face upon the pavement crying that His mercy endureth for ever. Centuries later that mercy stood on another pavement in a purple robe, and endured. The pavement of Gabbatha is the price of the pavement of 2Ch 7:3; the worship on the one was purchased by the silence on the other. And Ahaz’s small vandalism warns us how easily men lose the first: he did not abolish worship, he only rearranged the furniture, setting the brasen sea on a pavement of stones to please the king of Assyria. Worship is rarely destroyed at a stroke. It is amended, adjusted, and modernized, one convenient alteration at a time, until the pattern God gave is gone and no one remembers when.
roots_summary: Hebrew ritspah, a pavement of set stones, from a root meaning to fit together; Greek lithostrōton, “stone-strewn,” answering the Hebrew Gabbatha, an elevated place.
roots_lines: Hebrew — ritspah (רצפה), a pavement of fitted stones; the temple court floor of 2Ch 7:3 and Est 1:6.
Hebrew — the same consonants give ritspah, a live coal (Isa 6:6), from the sense of something set or laid in place.
Greek — lithostrōton (λιθόστρωτον), a floor paved with stones or mosaic; the name of Pilate’s tribunal court.
Aramaic — Gabbatha, the Hebrew name John records, understood as a ridge or raised place; the two names describe the same spot differently.
Latin — pavimentum, from pavire, to beat down; a floor rammed hard and then laid with stone.
usage: “They bowed with their faces to the ground upon the pavement when the glory filled the house.”
“Pilate sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement — and the Judge of all stood before him.”
“Ahaz did not abolish the worship; he only moved the sea onto a pavement of stones, and that was enough.”
